newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ retains foreign investment curbs in MIA talks.
newsitem.headline: NZ retains foreign investment curbs in MIA talks.

text.p: The New Zealand government would preserve current controls over foreign investment, including the power to decline proposals if they were not in the national interest, in any agreement under of the OECD's multilateral agreement on investment (MIA), Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Wednesday.
"The government's approach to the MIA specifically reserves current controls (exercised by) the Overseas Investment Commission," Bolger told parliament in answer to opposition questions.
Opposition Alliance Party leader Jim Anderton had accused the government of negotiating a secret deal which would be "a recipe for open slather (foreign acquisition)" in the MIA talks.

However, papers released by the government showed it planned to reserve the powers to approve investment currently exercised by the commission, retain the limits on foreign investments in companies like Telecom New Zealand, and maintain the ban on foreign investors owning fishing quotaS.
It also proposed a general reservation to protect the right to offer special treatment to Maori in settling their historical claims.
Anderton said he believed the MIA negotiations should be referred to parliament for ratification.
But Treasurer Winston Peters said in a statement that the talks had been handled in the same way as other treaties.
"New Zealand's foreign investment screening regime places a significant level of control on the activities of foreign individuals and companies, and that will not change," Peters said.
The MIA is being negotiated within the OECD to establish uniform rules for the liberalisation of foreign investment.
OECD ministers launched the negotiations in May 1995. The original May 1997 deadline set by officials for concluding the talks is likely to be extended, government papers said.
